topic: Flood-control master plans and integrated Metro Manila drainage planning
summary: Rep. Chel Diokno established that DPWH did not have a consolidated national flood-control and drainage plan, although the agency maintained master plans for all 18 major river basins and was updating 14 of them. DPWH said the updates were targeted for the first half of 2027 and supported a national legislative framework while favoring river-basin and locality-level implementation. Rep. Edgar Erice pressed for an integrated Metro Manila plan, and DPWH said an NCR-wide master-plan update would be completed by the end of the year or early the following year, with coordination among local-government plans. Rep. Renee Co cited the 2016 audit concerns and asked about delayed planning and projects that might worsen flooding; DPWH said audits and investigations were ongoing. An Iloilo member sought priority for floodway and drainage studies, and DPWH confirmed 102,000,000 for the feasibility-study update, although the stated combined total of 150,000,000 or 152,000,000 was not resolved.
question: The committee sought to establish whether DPWH had a national flood-control and drainage plan, how river-basin and urban plans were being coordinated, and when outdated plans would be completed. Members also asked whether Metro Manila had an integrated, NCR-wide plan and whether specific local studies and floodway projects would be funded and prioritized.
agency_position: DPWH said a single nationwide flood-control plan was not the preferred operational model; experts had recommended master plans by major river basin and locality, supported by common national principles. The agency nevertheless supported a national framework and committed to updating the 18 major river-basin plans and completing or finalizing an NCR-wide flood-mitigation plan, while coordinating with local governments.
outcome: DPWH gave planning and timing assurances, including updates to the 18 major river-basin plans and an NCR-wide master plan, and confirmed 102,000,000 for the Iloilo feasibility-study update. However, the national-versus-river-basin planning question, the final Metro Manila governance and coordination mechanism, the alleged project-selection problems, and the discrepancy between 150,000,000 and 152,000,000 remained open.

positions.position: A national framework of general principles was necessary to support rational, comprehensive flood-control and drainage planning, even if specific interventions were organized by river basin and locality.
Metro Manila needed an integrated waterways, drainage, waste, housing, transport, and traffic strategy with one accountable responsibility center rather than disconnected local-government plans.
The prolonged delay in completing updated flood-control master plans required explanation, and DPWH needed to examine whether project selection had produced projects that worsened flooding.
Iloilo's floodway feasibility study, drainage master-plan update, and related flood-mitigation projects should receive funding and priority under DPWH's reformulated prioritization system.
River-basin and locality-level plans were the technically appropriate approach, supplemented by nationwide principles and a national legislative framework.

topic: Ghost, substandard, and ineffective flood-control projects
summary: Rep. Chel Diokno questioned the absence of a consolidated national flood-control plan, and Secretary Vince Dizon defended the river-basin and urban-center approach while committing to update the plans by 2027. Members also pressed DPWH on lifestyle checks, contractor disclosures, convergence-program reforms, and nature-based solutions; the agency cited a one-strike policy, 12 blacklisted contractors, and proposed stronger disclosure rules. Rep. Antonio Tinio examined project vetting and central-office allocations, including the 50,000,000 threshold for central implementation, while DPWH cited certificates of implementability, geotagged photographs, and other documentation. Rep. Renee Co raised delayed master plans and projects that may have worsened flooding, and DPWH said audits with investigative agencies were ongoing. Rep. Stephen James Tan asked for the number of ghost projects; DPWH identified two areas, while the member characterized the situation as roughly 10 projects across two districts and about 183 engineering districts. DPWH reported 76% of contracts advertised, 32% awarded, and an 80% target by the end of September, but the ghost-project inventory and the status of flood-aggravating projects remained unresolved.
question: The committee sought to establish whether DPWH had adequate nationwide or river-basin flood-control plans, and whether its systems could prevent ghost, double-funded, substandard, or ineffective projects. Members also asked how projects were vetted and audited, how contractors and personnel were disciplined, how appropriations were distributed and implemented, and what reforms or reports DPWH would provide.
agency_position: DPWH said it was pursuing river-basin and urban-center master plans rather than a single consolidated national plan, while applying common flood-mitigation principles nationwide. It said it had instituted stricter project documentation, certificates of implementability, geotagging, contractor disclosures, blacklisting, audits, and convergence-program reforms, but acknowledged that the systems were not foolproof and that ghost, substandard, planning, and implementation problems remained under assessment.
outcome: DPWH presented reforms and gave commitments to update plans, submit a ghost-project report, strengthen contractor disclosures, and continue audits. The existence and extent of ghost and flood-aggravating projects remained under investigation, and the committee did not receive a final nationwide inventory or definitive resolution.

positions.position: A comprehensive national framework and updated flood-control plans were necessary, along with stronger transparency, lifestyle checks, accountability systems, and nature-based solutions.

Project vetting, traceability, district allocations, and central-office implementation required scrutiny because weak documentation or allocation practices could enable double funding or ghost projects.

Contractors and personnel linked to questionable, substandard, or ghost projects needed to be disciplined, and long-delayed master plans and projects that worsened flooding required audit and corrective action.
The committee needed a nationwide accounting of ghost projects and stronger planning and spending controls, while infrastructure spending should continue without sacrificing project quality.
He supported DPWH's reform program and urged the department to continue pursuing practical, reasonable, and important projects.

topic: Distribution of DPWH projects between districts, regions, and central office
summary: Rep. Cherilyn Banias Lugrales raised concerns about weak engineering studies, consultant accountability, district project implementation, and earthquake rehabilitation. Secretary Vince Dizon said proper studies ideally required 5% to 6% of capital outlay—roughly about 30 billion based on 460,000,000,000—but only 6,000,000,000 was budgeted for those activities, and he committed to report on project and rehabilitation concerns. Rep. Antonio Tinio questioned project traceability, leadership and district allocables, and the concentration of funds in the central office; Dizon cited certificates of implementability, geotagging, LGU coordination, and the 50,000,000 implementation threshold. A minority member questioned unusually uniform evacuation-center and social-facility allocations and wide district disparities, but the agency's explanation of five-year planning and interagency site identification did not fully resolve the basis for all allocations. Tinio also questioned why projects were distributed among only some of the 1,099 district engineering offices and warned that amendments and insertions could contribute to delays. Dizon committed to submit reports, justify changes, and move toward stricter, more consolidated and multiyear flood-control programming.
question: The committee sought to establish whether DPWH projects were properly vetted, traceable, and allocated on a needs-based basis among district engineering offices, regional offices, and the central office. Members also questioned whether fragmented project allocations and congressional changes contributed to duplication, weak accountability, and delays, particularly in flood control and post-earthquake rehabilitation.
agency_position: DPWH said project distribution was governed by certifications of implementability, LGU and RDC coordination, geotagged documentation, and DBM thresholds, with projects above 50,000,000 generally implemented centrally and projects below 50,000,000 generally assigned to district engineering offices. The agency acknowledged that central management and fragmented flood-control implementation were not yet ideal, said it was moving toward stricter and more coordinated programming, and supported multiyear appropriations.
outcome: The agency provided explanations for its vetting controls and central-versus-district implementation rules, but several allocation questions remained open. DPWH undertook to submit reports, verify project and accountability information, address earthquake rehabilitation, justify later changes, and pursue more coherent multiyear flood-control programming.

topic: Fragmented flood-control projects versus concentrated flagship investments
summary: Minority members questioned the basis for district and regional allocations and argued that flood-control funding should respond to need, hazard exposure, and project readiness rather than political or district distribution. They cited annual district allocations ranging from about 36,000,000 to 18 billion, as well as a 2022–2025 allocation of about 8.1 billion for Quezon City's 4th District. A member also criticized flood-control projects below 50,000,000 as fragmented and proposed concentrating resources in a flagship program for priority areas. Secretary Vince Dizon said centralized management was ideal, acknowledged that the current arrangement was not yet ideal, and pointed to stricter controls. He committed DPWH to environmental-impact studies for flood-mitigation projects affecting waterways and agreed that multiyear appropriations were the best solution, leaving the specific allocation formula unresolved.
question: The committee sought to establish whether flood-control funding should be allocated through fragmented district-level projects or concentrated in priority areas under a flagship, needs-based program. It also examined whether environmental-impact and project-preparation requirements should govern flood-control allocations.
agency_position: DPWH acknowledged that centrally managed and concentrated flood-mitigation programming was ideal and said it was moving toward stricter, more coordinated programming. Secretary Vince Dizon supported multiyear appropriations and committed to environmental-impact studies for flood-mitigation projects affecting waterways, but did not provide a complete resolution of district-level allocation disparities or fragmented projects.
outcome: The agency agreed in principle with more centralized, needs-based, environmentally screened, and multiyear flood-control programming, but the hearing did not settle the specific allocation formula or eliminate fragmented district-level projects. DPWH made a commitment on environmental-impact studies and endorsed multiyear appropriations.

positions.position: Flood-control allocations should be based on demonstrated need, hazard exposure, population, existing facilities, and project preparation rather than political or district-driven distribution.

topic: Flood-control facilities, pumping stations, detention basins, and water diversion
summary: Rep. Chel Diokno established that DPWH did not have a single consolidated national flood-control plan, although all 18 major river basins had plans and 14 were being updated, with completion targeted for 2027. Secretary Vince Dizon defended a river-basin and locality-based approach, while supporting detention basins, nature-based measures such as gabions, and upstream interventions. Rep. Roy Gonzales sought a Silang-Santa Rosa diversion or spillway solution, and DPWH cited 82,000,000 for a related feasibility study and undertook to pursue the study next year. Members raised Metro Manila detention sites, Pampanga pumping stations and bridges, Iloilo floodway studies, and dredging; DPWH committed to maintain or complete facilities, confirmed 102,000,000 for the Iloilo study update, and described dredging as a regular maintenance need. The hearing produced several agency commitments, but detention-facility performance targets and the final funding and sequencing of some projects remained unresolved.
question: The committee sought to establish whether DPWH had a coherent national and river-basin flood-control plan, how proposed detention, diversion, pumping, dredging, and nature-based facilities would be prioritized and maintained, and whether specific local projects would receive funding or completion commitments. Members also asked for technical studies, measurable flood-mitigation targets, and updates on unfinished facilities and bridges.
agency_position: DPWH said its flood-control strategy was based on major river-basin and urban-center master plans rather than a single technically uniform national plan, while applying common principles such as upstream interventions, detention basins, needs-based protection, and nature-based measures. The department presented detention facilities, diversion studies, pumping stations, dredging and desilting, and completion of unfinished structures as active or intended priorities, but several site-specific projects remained subject to feasibility studies, technical review, funding, or approval.
outcome: The agency answered the principal planning and technical questions and made commitments on plan updates, the Silang-Santa Rosa study, pumping stations, unfinished bridges, Iloilo studies, and regular dredging. However, the measurable targets for detention facilities, final project sequencing, and funding or approval of several local facilities remained open.

outcome: DPWH explained that the projects were subjected to additional vetting and that funds for projects deemed unimplementable or abandoned were treated as savings under the GAA general provisions. topic: MVUC and the discontinued stand-alone Special Road Fund
summary: Rep. Sidhu Ongwam questioned why the stand-alone Special Road Fund had disappeared from the FY 2027 PAP schedule and been placed under Asset Preservation. He cited the prior amount of 14,833,952,000 and the FY 2027 amount of 15,000,000,000, arguing that the new presentation made the earmarked fund less visible and could narrow its use because bridges were in a separate PAP. DPWH Undersecretary Nick Conti answered that Republic Act 11239 limited MVUC to roads, bridges, and road drainage and that qualifying projects under Asset Preservation Organizational Outcome No. 1 were attributed to MVUC. The agency said the 15,000,000,000 amount had been specified by DBM and offered to submit the detailed project list. Ongwam also raised constitutional, Supreme Court, and prior veto-message concerns, but those issues were not directly resolved. The immediate result was an agency commitment to provide supporting project documentation.

agency_position: DPWH stated that the MVUC collections were attributed to qualifying Asset Preservation projects under Organizational Outcome No. 1, consistent with the statutory scope under Republic Act 11239, and that the amount identified by DBM for 2027 was 15,000,000,000. The agency offered to furnish the committee with the detailed list of projects, but did not directly resolve whether DPWH requested the presentation or whether DBM imposed it, nor did it directly answer the constitutional and statutory concerns raised by Ongwam.
outcome: DPWH explained that the 2027 MVUC amount was attributed to qualifying Asset Preservation projects and undertook to provide the project list. The committee's concerns about the loss of a stand-alone line, the treatment of bridges, and the constitutional and statutory implications remained open.

thread.said: The DPWH official referred the question to Undersecretary Nick Conti. The response did not directly state whether DPWH requested the treatment or whether DBM imposed it.

thread.speaker: Undersecretary Nick Conti
thread.said: Conti explained that, following the amendment of Republic Act 8794 by Republic Act 11239, MVUC use was limited to the construction, upgrading, repair, and rehabilitation of roads, bridges, and road drainage. He said qualifying projects under Organizational Outcome No. 1 for Asset Preservation were attributed to MVUC collections, which were to be remitted to the Treasury under a special account in the General Fund.

thread.speaker: Undersecretary Nick Conti
thread.said: Conti said DPWH could furnish the committee with a list of the projects under Asset Preservation, Organizational Outcome No. 1, attributed to MVUC. He said the list would cover the amount specified by DBM for 2027.

thread.speaker: Undersecretary Nick Conti
thread.said: Conti identified the amount specified by DBM for 2027 as 15,000,000,000.

thread.speaker: Rep. Sidhu Ongwam
thread.said: Ongwam asked whether the Special Road Fund was a special fund under Article VI, Section 29(3) of the Constitution, consisting of money collected for a special purpose and payable only for that purpose. He contrasted it with Asset Preservation, which he characterized as a regular DPWH program funded through the General Appropriations Act.

thread.speaker: Rep. Sidhu Ongwam
thread.said: Ongwam argued that MVUC covered roads, bridges, and road drainage, while the FY 2027 Asset Preservation PAP covered preventive maintenance and rehabilitation of roads and drainage, with bridges in a separate Bridge Program. He asked whether placing MVUC within Asset Preservation narrowed the operative use of the statutory earmark because bridges were no longer within the PAP carrying the MVUC amount.

thread.speaker: Rep. Sidhu Ongwam
thread.said: Ongwam questioned the requirement that DPWH disaggregate Asset Preservation and submit to Congress a list of regular and MVUC-funded projects within fifteen days after effectivity. He said a post-effectivity report would not inform deliberations before enactment and argued that retaining a stand-alone Special Road Fund PAP would make the 15,000,000,000 visible without the need for later disaggregation.

thread.speaker: Rep. Sidhu Ongwam
thread.said: Ongwam characterized the fifteen-day disaggregation requirement as a workaround created by removing the stand-alone PAP. He further warned that post-enactment project identification had already been struck down by the Supreme Court.

thread.speaker: Rep. Sidhu Ongwam
thread.said: Ongwam informed the committee that a pending Supreme Court case challenged the constitutionality of unprogrammed funds, automatic appropriations, and earmarked funds such as special accounts in the General Fund and use of income in the General Fund, which he said included the Special Road Fund. He said the Court had already heard oral arguments five times and noted rulings that a General Appropriations Act could not amend a special law.

thread.speaker: DPWH agency official
thread.said: The official cited Republic Act 11239 and said MVUC proceeds were limited to the construction, upgrading, repair, and rehabilitation of roads, bridges, and road drainage, including safety, lighting, and cat's eye. The official said the 15,000,000,000 identified by DBM for 2027 was in Asset Preservation Organizational Outcome 001.

thread.speaker: DPWH agency official
thread.said: The official said the projects were detailed and itemized in the submitted National Expenditure Program and could be submitted to the committee. The official maintained that the projects were already reflected in the NEP.

thread.speaker: Rep. Sidhu Ongwam
thread.said: Ongwam recalled that in 2023 MVUC had likewise been included in Asset Preservation, but that the veto message stated the arrangement was allowed for that year and would not be allowed in succeeding years. He told the DPWH official that addressing this precedent was the agency's assignment.

topic: Project vetting, feasibility studies, and detailed engineering capacity
summary: Rep. Cherilyn Banias Lugrales questioned DPWH's allocation for detailed engineering and geotechnical studies, consultant accountability, and the basis for earthquake rehabilitation projects. Secretary Vince Dizon said the ideal allocation was about 5% to 6% of capital outlay—roughly about 30 billion based on the cited 2026 capital outlay—but only 6 billion was budgeted for the studies. He also acknowledged that DPWH lacked the personnel and specialized equipment needed to conduct studies for all 11,000 proposed 2027 projects. Rep. Antonio Tinio examined project traceability, certificates of implementability, geotagged documentation, and the central-office implementation of projects above the 50 million threshold. A congresswoman secured commitments for lists of feasibility-study and tourism-road projects and was told that projects costing 1 billion and above required a feasibility study. DPWH said tourism-road identification would be led by the concerned department, with joint technical validation with DPWH, while foreign-assisted and convergence projects would continue under documented implementation arrangements.
question: The committee sought to establish whether DPWH had sufficient funding, personnel, systems, and accountability mechanisms for feasibility studies, detailed engineering, geotechnical investigations, and project validation. Members also asked how projects were assigned, technically validated, and implemented, including convergence and foreign-assisted projects.
agency_position: DPWH said proper feasibility studies, detailed engineering, geotechnical work, certificates of implementability, geotagged documentation, and local-government coordination were necessary safeguards, but acknowledged that funding, personnel, and specialized equipment were insufficient for the full project workload. The agency maintained that implementation generally followed DBM thresholds and program-specific rules, with joint validation for convergence projects and commitments to submit requested lists and reports.
outcome: DPWH acknowledged substantial gaps in study funding and internal technical capacity, while defending its project-vetting and implementation controls. The department undertook to provide lists, reports, and follow-up on consultant accountability and earthquake rehabilitation, but the adequacy of funding, the final responsibility for some projects, and the accountability record remained open.

positions.position: DPWH should strengthen in-house engineering and geotechnical capacity, improve consultant accountability, and ensure earthquake rehabilitation projects were based on actual damage inventories.

Project proposals needed more complete documentation, traceability, location information, and safeguards against double funding and ghost projects; the basis for central-office implementation and district allocations also required scrutiny.
Feasibility-study funding and responsibility for tourism-road identification and validation should be clearly documented under the new convergence arrangements.
Convergence and foreign-assisted projects should meet documentation, geotagging, certification, and approved-program-of-work requirements, while DPWH reforms should continue.

thread.speaker: Rep. Cherilyn Banias Lugrales

thread.said: Using the 2026 capital-outlay figure of 460,000,000,000, Dizon said 5% to 6% would be roughly about 30,000,000,000, while the 2026 budget for these studies was only 6,000,000,000.

thread.speaker: Rep. Cherilyn Banias Lugrales

He said the department needed geologists, geotechnical engineers, and specialized equipment that it did not currently have.

thread.speaker: Rep. Cherilyn Banias Lugrales

thread.speaker: Secretary Vince Dizon
thread.said: Dizon said he would have the regional director and district engineering office address the concern. He committed to addressing yellow-tagged and red-tagged school buildings and health facilities through the department's funds, including the End-.... thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: Tinio presented project-vetting and budget-reform concerns, emphasizing technical review, information, traceability, transparency, and protection against randomly proposed or unsupported projects.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: Using a district-engineering-office proposal for road construction with a stated amount of 5,000,000 and a total proposal of more or less 404,000,000, he asked whether the documentation met the Secretary's objectives for traceability and complete project information.

thread.speaker: Secretary Vince Dizon
thread.said: Dizon said BIP projects were coordinated with local government units and required certifications from the LDC, PDC, or RDC, including certificates of implementability. He said these requirements were intended to establish accountability and prevent unsupported projects.

thread.speaker: Secretary Vince Dizon
thread.said: Dizon identified the certificate of implementability, DEO review, project-title and budget information, and geotagged on-site photographs as safeguards against double funding and ghost projects. He said engineers uploaded location information and real-time photographs to the system.

thread.speaker: Secretary Vince Dizon
thread.said: Dizon acknowledged that no protection was 100% foolproof, mentioning the possibility of manipulated map or photographic materials, but said the requirements provided layers of protection.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: Tinio asked whether road proposals should identify locations and station markings, including standard markings every 200 meters, to make project descriptions and validation more precise.

thread.speaker: Secretary Vince Dizon

thread.speaker: Secretary Vince Dizon
thread.said: Dizon said the 2027 process prioritized regions and districts and that 80% of the more than 11,000 projects had RDC endorsement. He said RDC endorsement was required from the relevant districts and regions and that the distribution among legislative districts followed a formula.

topic: Major bridges, inter-island connectivity, and multiyear completion funding
summary: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez sought support for Cagayan de Oro bypass roads and bridges, citing about 34 billion for the Coastal Bypass Road, about 7 billion for the Eastern Interior Road, and additional funding for local bridges and walkways. He also highlighted feasibility-study funding for the Mindanao-Visayas connection, including 350 million for the Surigao-to-Southern Leyte bridge study. Rep. Sarah Elago questioned the status of 944 TCAS projects and the ADB Metro Manila Bridges Project, citing more than 3 billion pesos in disbursements and requesting detailed records, traffic studies, blueprints, and compensation information. Secretary Dizon said DPWH would verify the project information and submit the requested reports, except that the MRT 7 blueprint would be referred to DOTR. Rep. Salvador Pleyto and Rep. Timothy Titan pressed for complete multiyear bridge funding, earthquake assessment, anti-overloading enforcement, and safety improvements. Rep. Anna York Bondoc raised unfinished Pampanga pumping stations and bridges, including the 95%-complete Delta Bridge; Secretary Dizon committed to fund and finish the facilities and said the Delta Bridge would be completed by early the following year.
question: The committee sought to establish which major bridge, bypass-road, flood-control, and inter-island connectivity projects required funding; whether projects would be completed rather than left in phases; and what schedules, feasibility studies, project records, and implementation responsibilities applied.
agency_position: DPWH said it was moving toward multiyear appropriations with clear completion timelines for bridges and other major projects, while continuing to seek foreign or counterpart financing for feasibility studies and large infrastructure. The agency acknowledged that several project statuses and records required verification, but committed to provide reports, studies, lists, and other documents and to prioritize or complete unfinished bridges and pumping facilities.
outcome: The agency gave policy assurances on multiyear bridge appropriations and committed to complete or prioritize unfinished bridges and the Delta Bridge, while undertaking to submit numerous project reports and records. Several TCAS, ADB bridge, right-of-way, and feasibility-study details remained subject to agency verification or later submission.

positions.position: Supported increasing the DPWH budget and sought funding and foreign financing for Cagayan de Oro bypass roads, bridges, walkways, and the Mindanao-Visayas inter-island connection.
Pressed DPWH for documentary accountability on TCAS and the ADB Metro Manila Bridges Project, including project status, disbursements, traffic effects, blueprints, and compensation.
Advocated complete, start-to-finish funding for long bridges and requested earthquake-retrofitting and structural-integrity information for Metro Manila infrastructure.
Supported evidence-based feasibility studies, requested a list of major projects, and sought clarity on responsibility for tourism-road identification, validation, and implementation.
Called for stronger anti-overloading enforcement, additional weighing facilities, multiyear bridge funding, and pedestrian overpasses for road safety.
Urged completion and funding of Pampanga pumping stations, unfinished bridges, bypass roads, and the Delta Bridge because of flooding, connectivity, and national-security concerns.

topic: Earthquake rehabilitation, bridge safety, and seismic retrofitting
summary: Rep. Cherilyn Banias Lugrales questioned DPWH's allocation and capacity for geotechnical and detailed engineering studies, citing earthquake-related structural damage and soil-liquefaction risks. Secretary Vince Dizon said the department ideally needed 5% to 6% of capital outlay for such work—roughly about 30 billion based on 460 billion—but had only 6 billion in 2026. He acknowledged that DPWH lacked the personnel and equipment to conduct studies for all 11,000 proposed 2027 projects and committed to seek additional funds and report on consultant accountability and procurement requirements. Lugrales also raised her district's reduction from about 1.7 billion to more or less 500 million after a 7.8 earthquake, and Dizon committed to having regional and district officials address rehabilitation of yellow- and red-tagged facilities. Rep. Jonathan Keith Flores raised a dangerous critical bridge whose delays cost around 147 million per day, and Dizon cited retrofit and replacement amounts, including 150,000,000 and unclear figures spoken as 150.20 26 and 600,000,020.27. Rep. Salvador Pleyto requested plans for retrofitting critical infrastructure and inspecting buildings for the West Valley Fault risk, and Dizon committed to submit the ongoing World Bank-funded NCR assessment.
question: The committee sought to establish whether DPWH had adequate resources, technical capacity, and accountability mechanisms for geotechnical studies and the rehabilitation or retrofitting of earthquake-damaged and critical bridges. It also sought commitments on completing bridge projects, assessing critical infrastructure, and reporting measurable resilience and rehabilitation plans.
agency_position: DPWH acknowledged that funding and capacity for feasibility studies, detailed engineering, and geotechnical investigations were inadequate, and that the department was not yet equipped to perform all studies internally. It stated that it would address earthquake-damaged facilities, pursue retrofit or replacement of critical bridges through a nationwide strategy, use multiyear appropriations for major projects, and submit the ongoing World Bank-funded NCR assessment.
outcome: DPWH gave assurances on district rehabilitation, critical-bridge retrofit or replacement, and a nationwide bridge strategy, but several requested details remained subject to verification, reports, or ongoing assessments. The World Bank-funded NCR assessment and specific rehabilitation and accountability information had not yet been submitted during the hearing.

positions.position: DPWH should strengthen geotechnical and engineering studies, develop internal technical expertise instead of relying excessively on consultants, ensure consultant accountability, and base earthquake rehabilitation funding on a documented inventory of damaged facilities.
The dangerous condition of the critical bridge he raised required immediate DPWH action because crossing delays imposed substantial economic costs on multiple regions.

DPWH should provide a clear plan for retrofitting critical infrastructure and inspecting national buildings before a major earthquake, and major bridge projects should be funded through completion rather than left unfinished through fragmented packaging.

topic: National-road maintenance and post-construction asset preservation
summary: Rep. Sidhu Ongwam questioned why the MVUC special road fund was no longer displayed as a standalone FY 2027 program and argued that embedding it in Asset Preservation reduced legislative visibility. DPWH Undersecretary Nick Conti and Secretary Vince Dizon said the amount was attributed to itemized Asset Preservation projects pursuant to the statutory limits on MVUC use and identified the 2027 amount as about 15 billion. DPWH undertook to furnish the committee with the relevant project lists, but the record did not resolve Ongwam's concerns about bridges, post-enactment disaggregation, or the legality of the presentation. Rep. Michael Pan raised right-of-way and routine and post-construction maintenance problems affecting national highways, particularly in Samar. The secretary committed to address post-construction maintenance and said national roads remained DPWH's primary mandate, while local-road concerns involving remote and island municipalities were left for continuing coordination with regional and district offices.
question: The committee sought to establish whether the motor vehicle users charge (MVUC) collections were properly and visibly appropriated for their statutory purposes, including roads, bridges, and drainage. Members also sought assurance that DPWH would adequately fund routine and post-construction maintenance of national highways while addressing right-of-way and local-road concerns in remote areas.
agency_position: DPWH stated that the 2027 MVUC amount was attributed to itemized projects under Asset Preservation Organizational Outcome No. 1 and remained limited to the statutory purposes of construction, upgrading, repair, and rehabilitation of roads, bridges, and road drainage. The department said it could furnish the committee with the project list and undertook to address post-construction maintenance, while maintaining that national roads were its primary mandate and local roads would be considered through regional and district offices.
outcome: DPWH explained that the 15,000,000,000 MVUC amount was attributed to itemized Asset Preservation projects and undertook to provide supporting project information, but the committee's concerns about visibility, the treatment of bridges, and possible statutory or constitutional issues were not definitively resolved. DPWH separately committed to address post-construction maintenance, while the broader Samar local-road and right-of-way concerns remained subject to further agency action.

positions.position: He objected to the disappearance of the standalone special road fund line, arguing that embedding the 15,000,000,000 MVUC amount in Asset Preservation reduced legislative visibility and potentially raised statutory and constitutional concerns.

He urged stronger funding and action for right-of-way, routine and post-construction maintenance of national highways, and local-road infrastructure in Samar and other remote or island municipalities.

He maintained that DPWH should prioritize national roads but indicated that the department would address the post-construction maintenance concern and continue working through regional directors and district engineers on local-road concerns.

topic: Transparency, contractor accountability, and anti-corruption controls
summary: Rep. Iris Marie Montes asked Secretary Vince Dizon to make DPWH project information, procurement records, financial data, monitoring results, contractor ratings, and complaints publicly accessible. Dizon said the Transparency Portal already covered completed and ongoing projects, bidding livestreams, satellite-based monitoring, and supporting documents for PLN 11,000 plus projects, and committed to quarterly reports. Rep. Chel Diokno pressed DPWH on the absence of a consolidated national flood-control plan, lifestyle checks, contractor disclosures, convergence-program reforms, and nature-based solutions; Dizon cited plans for all 18 major river basins, with 14 being updated, and a target of 2027 for completion. Rep. Renee Co asked about blacklisting, delayed master plans, and audits, and DPWH reported 12 blacklisted contractors and ongoing investigations. Eli San Fernando questioned Redicon and R2 Builders, including figures of 9,000,000,000 and 2,700,000,000 pesos, and raised an alleged worker-wage shortfall involving 60 pesos over an 85 pesos rate. The agency's response on that allegation was garbled, leaving that issue unresolved.
question: The committee sought to establish whether DPWH had effective transparency, disclosure, monitoring, auditing, and contractor-accountability mechanisms to protect public funds. Members also asked what information would be published, how anti-corruption controls were being implemented, and whether DPWH would act on questionable contracts, project quality, and worker-wage compliance.
agency_position: DPWH said it was institutionalizing transparency through a public portal containing project, bidding, monitoring, and supporting documentation, while developing quarterly reporting, enhanced disclosures, and closer coordination with the Ombudsman, SEC, and investigative agencies. It also defended river-basin-based planning and program reforms, reported that 12 contractors had been blacklisted, and said audits and master-plan updates were ongoing; however, the response on R2 Builders' wage compliance was unclear.
outcome: The agency made commitments on quarterly portal reporting, enhanced contractor disclosures, nature-based-solution reporting, master-plan updates, and submission of contractor information. Blacklisting and audits were reported as ongoing, but the wage-compliance allegation involving R2 Builders and several details concerning contractor accountability remained unresolved.

positions.position: She supported a comprehensive, publicly accessible project-transparency system covering procurement, project implementation, financial accountability, contractor performance, and citizen complaints, and sought regular reporting on anti-corruption results.

He pressed for a comprehensive national framework for flood-control and drainage planning, systematic lifestyle checks and disclosures, scrutiny of convergence programs, and inclusion of nature-based solutions.
She pressed DPWH to hold contractors and project personnel accountable for questionable or substandard flood-control projects and criticized delays in producing updated master plans.
He questioned the scale of Redicon and R2 Builders' contracts and argued that contractors receiving billions in public contracts should comply with worker-wage obligations.

He maintained that DPWH had begun meaningful transparency, disclosure, contractor-review, program-streamlining, and audit reforms, while acknowledging that some systems and plans remained under development.

topic: Classroom construction, evacuation centers, and social-facility appropriations
summary: A minority member questioned the specificity and allocation basis of regional appropriations for evacuation centers, PWD facilities, and senior-citizen facilities, citing 180,000,000, 5,000,000, and 20,000,000. The agency said evacuation-center sites and amounts were governed by a five-year plan and required coordination, validation, and implementability checks, while the Chair requested a district-by-district breakdown. Congressman Joseph Tan discussed project convergence, foreign-assisted projects, and a total DPWH amount of about 200 plus billion pesos, but the exchange did not produce a detailed accounting. Another member said only 30% of the FY2026 budget had been awarded and warned that the delay threatened the 6,000-classroom target. Secretary Vince Dizon corrected the reported classroom data and cited a 20,000,000,000 DPWH budget for 6,000 classrooms, while explaining that construction commonly began in the third quarter after validation and bidding. agency_position: DPWH said project allocations were subject to implementability, site, coordination, and validation requirements, and that evacuation-center sites and amounts were determined under a five-year plan with other disaster-management agencies. On classrooms, DPWH said third-quarter starts and October-November bidding were longstanding consequences of coordination and validation, while supporting closer grouping of the budget with DepEd and clearer planning.
outcome: The Chair undertook to raise the proposal for clearer GAA line items, but the record did not resolve the disputed allocation basis, the district figures, or the classroom-award delay. The issue therefore remained open subject to the requested breakdown and further committee consideration.

positions.position: Vague regional and district allocations were not sufficiently needs-based or specific and required a district-level breakdown and stronger accountability.

topic: Pedestrian, bicycle, sidewalk, and PWD infrastructure
summary: Rep. Renee Co pressed DPWH to prioritize pedestrians and cyclists, separate pedestrian projects from general rehabilitation, and provide wider sidewalks, protected bike lanes, and improved PWD facilities. DPWH cited a pedestrian-walkway expansion cost of about 6 billion, an original EDSA project cost of about 17 billion, EDSA pedestrian widths ranging from a minimum of 2.8 meters to as much as five meters, and a minimum bike-lane width of 1.5 meters. Co also cited a total DPWH budget of roughly 644 billion and a 510 million allocation for PWD, elderly, senior, and gender-responsive facilities, while the secretary said the PWD budget would increase three times from 170 million. Rep. Timothy Titan then asked for stronger anti-overloading enforcement, additional weighing facilities, multiyear bridge funding, and two more pedestrian overpasses along the Maharlika Highway. Secretary Vince Dizon committed to doing his best to enforce anti-overloading rules and suggested multiyear bridge appropriations from 2027 onward, but no definitive action on the overpass request was recorded.
question: The committee sought to establish whether DPWH's FY2027 program adequately funded pedestrianization, protected bike lanes, wider sidewalks, and facilities for persons with disabilities, and whether the agency would address unsafe bridges, overloaded trucks, and requested pedestrian overpasses. Members also pressed DPWH on applicable standards, enforcement, and multiyear infrastructure planning.
agency_position: DPWH said pedestrian widths and bike-lane standards were being considered, but pedestrian facilities remained part of broader rehabilitation projects and were constrained by available space. The agency also supported stronger anti-overloading enforcement, indicated that multiyear bridge appropriations could be pursued from 2027 onward, and did not record a clear disposition on the requested pedestrian overpasses.
outcome: DPWH acknowledged the need for pedestrian, bicycle, and PWD facilities and indicated that the PWD allocation would increase, but pedestrian projects were still embedded in broader rehabilitation work. The secretary committed to anti-overloading enforcement and discussed multiyear bridge funding, while the pedestrian-overpass request remained without a recorded agency disposition.

positions.position: Pedestrians, cyclists, PWDs, and commuters should receive priority over a car-centric road approach, with separately identified and adequately funded pedestrianization, protected bike lanes, wider sidewalks, and accessible facilities.
DPWH should enforce anti-overloading rules more strictly, expand weighing facilities, consider multiyear bridge funding, and construct pedestrian overpasses at identified high-risk locations.
DPWH would seek to enforce anti-overloading regulations and pursue multiyear bridge appropriations, while the transcript does not establish a final position on the requested overpasses.

thread.speaker: Rep. Chel Diokno
thread.said: Rep. Diokno asked DPWH to respond to reports concerning major scam or ghost projects associated with the convergence and special support programs.

thread.speaker: Vince Dizon, DPWH official
thread.said: Dizon said DPWH had discussed the convergence and special programs with Secretary Babe Singhson and had incorporated reform recommendations into the proposed budget. He said the CPAG component had been removed, while the basic infrastructure program remained for mostly non-national or local roads, bridges, and other community infrastructure, with more stringent requirements.

thread.speaker: Vince Dizon, DPWH official
thread.said: Dizon said DPWH had also streamlined or removed other convergence-program portions, including Roll It and Trip C, because the departments primarily responsible for the sectors should identify the projects. He identified tourism for Trip C, DTI for Roll It, and other sector departments for their respective programs.

thread.speaker: Vince Dizon, DPWH official
thread.said: Dizon said assigning projects to lead departments would reduce the risk that program items would be used for purposes other than those originally intended, such as roads to tourist destinations or industrial parks. He said the reforms were not yet perfect but represented a step in the right direction.

thread.speaker: a congresswoman
thread.said: The congresswoman referred to a 2026 bridge item and asked about the proposed 2027 feasibility-study funding for the project. The transcript identifies the project as Sorcegon Summer Bridge, but the associated figures and wording are partly unclear.

thread.speaker: DPWH official
thread.said: The DPWH official said the feasibility study would involve foreign funding and counterpart funding, including a 130,000,000 counterpart amount associated with the Asian Development Bank, subject to the study's results before funding could be pursued.

thread.speaker: a congresswoman
thread.said: The congresswoman asked about the feasibility study for the Southern Gate to Surigao long-span bridge, which she said would connect the Visayas and Mindanao.

thread.speaker: DPWH official
thread.said: The DPWH official said 350,000,000 was provided for the feasibility study in 2027.

thread.speaker: a congresswoman
thread.said: The congresswoman asked DPWH to submit a list of major projects with feasibility-study funding and asked whether a minimum project-cost threshold applied before a full feasibility study was required.

thread.speaker: DPWH official
thread.said: The DPWH official agreed to submit the list. He said projects costing 1,000,000,000 and above required a feasibility study.

thread.speaker: a congresswoman
thread.said: The congresswoman asked about the transition of tourism-road projects under the reforms, particularly whether ongoing Trip C projects and their continuing appropriations would remain with DPWH.

thread.speaker: DPWH official
thread.said: The DPWH official said the department would submit a list of ongoing Trip C projects. The exchange indicated that ongoing projects and 2027 treatment were still being clarified, with references to DBM and the Department of Tourism.

thread.speaker: a congresswoman
thread.said: The congresswoman asked which department would have primary responsibility for identifying and prioritizing tourism roads under the new setup, and who would conduct technical validation and implementation.

thread.speaker: DPWH official
thread.said: The official said the concerned department would have primary responsibility for identifying and prioritizing tourism roads. Technical validation and implementation would be joint between that department and DPWH, similar to arrangements for classrooms and farm-to-market roads.

thread.speaker: Rep. Stephen James Tan
thread.said: Rep. Tan raised questions about the approval and implementation documents required for convergence and major projects, including approved plans of works, implementability documents, and certificates of non-objection. The machine-generated transcript is incomplete, but the focus was on project readiness and approval controls.

thread.speaker: DPWH official
thread.said: The DPWH response emphasized that convergence decisions should move toward primary responsibility by the department concerned: DPWH for its infrastructure, DTI for Roll It, DepEd for school-related projects, and DA for farm-to-market roads. The remainder of the answer is garbled, but it referred to transparency and flexibility for ongoing projects.

thread.speaker: Rep. Stephen James Tan
thread.said: Rep. Tan stated that the total amount for the DPWH family was "200 plus billion pesos."

thread.speaker: DPWH official
thread.said: The DPWH official confirmed that foreign-assisted critical projects were ongoing and referred to foreign-assisted projects for the following year. The details of the response are substantially garbled.

thread.speaker: Rep. Stephen James Tan
thread.said: Rep. Tan raised project clustering and referred to a figure described in the transcript as "Short page classroom more or less from 160,150." The question and the figure's context are unclear.

thread.speaker: DPWH official
thread.said: The DPWH response said clustering should consolidate projects by site or area while preserving quality and accounting for difficult locations such as mountainous areas. The official said there was no rigid rule and that clustering should serve the end goal.

thread.speaker: Anna Condo, a Pampanga member
thread.said: Rep. Condo asked DPWH to explain its dredging policy and provide more information about dredging and desilting as a flood-control intervention.

thread.speaker: Vince Dizon, DPWH official
thread.said: Dizon said dredging and desilting were critical initial flood-mitigation interventions. He said DPWH was pursuing a full-blast dredging and desilting program for major rivers and waterways and that this should become a regular DPWH maintenance program.

thread.speaker: Anna Condo, a Pampanga member
thread.said: Rep. Condo flagged the Korea-assisted flood-control project, particularly the unfinished second part after the inauguration of part one. She said the project could proceed in less than six months and asked that the Korean loan and its details be pursued.

thread.speaker: Vince Dizon, DPWH official
thread.said: Dizon referred to RDC approval in response to the Korea-assisted project issue. The transcript does not clearly state whether the approval had already been secured or what remaining steps were required.
